open-question.question: When the completion procedure's discretionary read of past work fails — its `tasks <path> --with-body` call or its `show <milestone path>` follow-up exits non-zero, as `show` does on the `-` a task line prints for a commit joining no single milestone — what does the runner do: stop the task on a fixed line with the tool's `Error:` line beneath it, as the review pass and the starting-state procedure stop on a failed read of theirs, or carry on with the task without the read, as `ask-in-milestone-context` carries on after telling the failure in prose?

When the completion procedure's read of past work surfaces an earlier milestone's decision or verified bar that carrying out the task as briefed would undo, and the current milestone's `requirements.md` does not address it, what governs the work: the brief as written, the earlier decision wherever the brief can still be met, or does the runner stop without completing the task?

When the completion procedure's step-2 read of past work fixes a criterion of the acceptance bar, does that criterion name what it was formed against (the task commit's hash or the earlier milestone's path), so the read shows in the `Task-completion:` commit body, or is it worded like any other criterion with no reference to the read?
open-question.alternative: A criterion the step-2 read fixes is worded like every other criterion of the bar, as an observable property of the deliverable with no hash, milestone path, or other mention of the read, the same way a criterion a prior task's live deliverable fixes is worded today. Step 2 gains no wording rule for it and step 5's form sentence stays exactly as it is. The bar stays what the task-altitude invariant calls it, a list of checkable properties and nothing beyond them, with no provenance in the text a later reader judges by. The procedure gets no new rule and no runner changes, and no criterion carries a reference that a rebase or amend could leave pointing at nothing. The read leaves no trace in the `Task-completion:` commit, so nothing in history shows a criterion came from past work or which earlier decision it keeps in force. Whether the read was taken can then be seen only in a run's transcript, which matters if the sibling measurement questions count outcomes from commits rather than from transcripts.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name what it was formed against, inside its own `- ` bullet: the abbreviated hash from the `tasks` line when a task commit's diff or bar fixed it, and the milestone path from that line's third field when a decision that `show` printed fixed it. Step 2 states the rule once, and step 5's form sentence lets a bullet carry it, so the body is still the bar alone, one bullet per criterion. Each such criterion points at its evidence directly: one `git show <hash>` or one `show <path>` takes a reader to exactly what fixed it, using the identifier the read itself used. The read shows in every `Task-completion:` body that `tasks --with-body` prints back, so the history records it without a transcript. Provenance goes into the bar text, which the project keeps out of recorded `## Decisions` prose on purpose, and a criterion becomes partly a citation rather than purely an observable property. An abbreviated hash stops resolving if a branch is rebased or amended before it merges, and the procedure has to state two reference forms and when each applies.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name, inside its own bullet, the milestone path from the third field of the `tasks` line the read went through, whether a task commit's bar or a decision `show` printed fixed it. No hash is ever named. A path is readable and survives rebase and amend, and `show` takes it exactly as written, so the reference stays meaningful as long as history does. One form serves both cases, and the rule takes a single sentence. It is coarser than the evidence: it names the milestone, not the task commit whose bar or diff actually fixed the criterion, so a reader has to search that milestone's tasks again. A task commit that joins no single milestone prints `-` in that field and leaves nothing to name, and a finished milestone's slug can be defined again at the same path later, so `show` on the path may then print a different milestone.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name, inside its own bullet, the abbreviated hash of the task commit from the `tasks` line it was formed against. That includes a criterion a `show` follow-up fixed, which names the hash of the task commit that led the read to that milestone. No milestone path is named. One uniform reference that always exists, since every read starts from a `tasks` line that prints a hash, including a commit whose milestone field is `-`. It is the most exact pointer: `git show` on it reaches the brief, the bar, and the diff, and from its milestone field the decision. A hash is opaque to someone reading the bar and does not name the decision when a decision rather than a task fixed the criterion, so that link takes a second hop. An abbreviated hash stops resolving after a rebase or amend of the branch, and it can become ambiguous as history grows.

A criterion the step-2 read fixes may name its source inside its own bullet, a hash for a task commit or a milestone path for a decision, when the runner judges that the reference helps a later reader. Otherwise it is worded like any other criterion. The procedure allows the reference and requires it nowhere. The runner can record provenance exactly where it explains a criterion that would otherwise look arbitrary, and keep the bar clean where the criterion speaks for itself, without a rule that fires on every read. Nothing can check it and nothing can rely on it. A body without a reference does not show that no read was taken, so the history cannot be used to count reads, and bodies differ from run to run in a way no reader or test can predict.

The criteria the step-2 read fixes are worded like every other criterion. The body instead ends with one trailing paragraph of `Token: value` lines, one per source the read used, holding the abbreviated hash for a task commit or the milestone path for a decision. The body contract and step 5's form sentence widen to allow this paragraph after the bullets, and both completion runners' body handling carries it. The bar text stays free of provenance, and `tasks --with-body`, `summary`, and `record` print it exactly as now, because every body the milestones tool prints already drops a trailing paragraph of `Token: value` lines. `git log` and `git show` still show which past work fed the bar. It breaks the invariant that the commit body is the bar and nothing else, and it requires edits to the step-5 form sentence and to both runners' calls. A trailer names sources for the bar as a whole, not for a particular criterion. And because the milestones tool drops it, no query through the tool shows the read: counting reads from it means a hand-written `git log`, the hand-rolled read the tool exists to replace.

open-question.question: The completion procedure's read of past work is triggered by a file the task edits rather than creates whose shape the milestone's `requirements.md` does not explain. Does the same trigger cover a file the task deletes, renames, or moves?
open-question.alternative: The trigger stays a change to the content of a file that already exists. `complete-procedure.md` says outright that deleting, renaming, or moving a file takes no read of past work, so the read is never taken for any of the three. A rename or move that also changes the file's content still triggers on that content edit, as any edit does. The trigger is the narrowest one and mechanically plain, so a runner never has to judge whether a removal counts. The sibling question on which runs the field measurement counts gets a clean population: runs that changed the content of a file that already existed. It also keeps the procedure's added text as small as the goal's one-sentence trigger. The most destructive change a task can make goes unchecked. Deleting or relocating a file that an earlier milestone deliberately placed (this repository has one: the host fixture's `milestones.fixture/` container is named so the discovery pattern skips it, and a `CLAUDE.md` invariant explains why) skips exactly the read meant to show why a file is the way it is. The brief and `requirements.md` are then the only guard.

The procedure treats deleting, renaming, or moving a file that already exists as editing it. The read is taken under the same condition as an edit: `requirements.md` does not explain the file's existence or place. It is taken at step 2 for files the task names up front and at step 3 for the rest. The query is `tasks` on the path the file has before the task. The milestones tool's log reads set `log.follow=false`, so the new path carries no history from before the move, while the old path, still in the tree when the read is taken, lists every task commit that changed it. Every change that undoes something already standing gets the same check before it is made. That includes removals, where an earlier decision that put the file there is most easily lost without anyone noticing. The tool needs no change: the old path exists in the tree when the read is taken, and `tasks` exits 0 on it whatever it lists. The trigger gets wider and the procedure's prose longer. It needs a clause naming which path to read, because reading the new path silently returns only the move commit. More completion runs then take a read whose output can be large: the sibling question on bounding large reads covers this. The measurement population sibling must decide whether these runs count.

The procedure treats deleting a file that already exists as editing it, under the same condition that `requirements.md` does not explain the file's existence. The read is `tasks` on that path, taken before the deletion. A pure rename or move, with the content unchanged, takes no read. The procedure says so, because the file's shape survives under its new path. The read targets the one case where the file's shape is lost outright and an earlier decision behind it cannot be seen in the tree afterwards. Renames and moves get no read, and no clause is needed about which path to read, since a deleted file has only the one path. Location can be a decision too: a name or place chosen so that a pattern matches or skips it, or a path other files cite. Such a decision is broken by a rename or move without a read. The line drawn between deletion and relocation is also one more distinction the runner has to apply and the measurement has to tell apart.

The procedure keeps the trigger worded as the goal states it, "a file the task edits rather than creates", and says nothing about deletions, renames, or moves. Whether one of these counts as an edit is left to the runner's reading on each run. The discretionary read is taken or not as that reading falls. No wording is added and no position is fixed before the field measurement has shown how runners actually treat these cases. The read is discretionary anyway, so the measurement can show whether a stated rule is needed. Runners will read "edits" differently, so the same deletion triggers the read in one run and not in another. For renames, a runner that does take the read may query the new path and get nothing, because the tool follows no rename. The measurement's counted population, owned by a sibling question, also becomes ambiguous for exactly these runs.

open-question.question: The completion procedure's read of past work is triggered by a file whose shape the milestone's `requirements.md` does not explain. Does a shape the project's context file explains (in this repository, a `CLAUDE.md` invariant) count as explained, so that no read is taken, or does only `requirements.md` count?
open-question.alternative: Only the milestone's `requirements.md` counts as explaining a file's shape: its goal, its `## Relevant starting state`, and its recorded decisions. What the context file says about the file, however fully it gives the reason (in this repository a `CLAUDE.md` invariant), does not count, so an edited file whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain triggers the `tasks <path> --with-body` read even when the context file explains it. The procedure says this in one clause of its trigger sentence. It matches the goal's wording exactly and gives a trigger a runner can check against one document already read whole at step 2. The read still fires on core files that a project's context file documents heavily, which is where an earlier milestone's decision most likely sits and where the context file's account can lag behind the task commits' bars. This keeps the measured population large enough to decide whether the read stays discretionary. In a project whose context file already gives the reason for a shape, the read repeats what the runner holds. It is paid at the measured sizes (200 lines, 59 KB for `docs/skill-reference.md`, 104 lines for `CLAUDE.md` itself), and in this repository it would fire on nearly every edit of a file under `core/` or `docs/`, since a milestone's `requirements.md` rarely explains files outside its own goal.

Both `requirements.md` and the workspace-root context file count, but the context file counts only where it states why the shape is as it is, for the part of the file the edit changes (for example an invariant giving the reason and saying what must not be restored). A context-file passage that only describes the file, such as a repository-layout entry naming what the file holds, does not count. A shape neither document gives a reason for triggers the read. The procedure says this in its trigger sentence, which then names the context file beside `requirements.md`. It skips the read exactly where the runner already holds the reason for the shape at no extra cost, since step 2 reads the context file whole. It also uses the protection the design draft relies on, finish writing lasting changes into the context file, rather than repeating it with a history read. A description-only mention still leaves the read in force. It goes beyond the goal's literal trigger, which names `requirements.md` alone. It also asks the runner to judge whether a context-file passage gives the reason for the specific element it is changing, which is softer than checking one document. In this repository, whose `CLAUDE.md` gives the reason for most core files, the read would rarely fire, which shrinks the runs the field measurement can count if its population is defined by the trigger.

Both `requirements.md` and the context file count, and the context file counts wherever it gives any account of the file's shape, a description included (a layout entry, a conventions paragraph), not only a stated reason. Only a file that neither document mentions in a way that accounts for its shape triggers the read. It is the easiest form to check. A runner only asks whether the file is accounted for in either document it read at step 2, so the read is reserved for files the project's own documentation leaves uncovered, and its cost on heavily documented files drops to nothing. A description says what a file is, not why an element of it was chosen, so the read is skipped on exactly the documented core files where an earlier milestone's deliberate choice is most likely to be undone. That brings back the risk the read exists to guard against. In this repository almost every tracked file has a `CLAUDE.md` layout entry, so the read would almost never fire.

Any project document the runner reads counts as explaining the shape: `requirements.md`, the context file, `README.md`, the project's docs (in this repository `docs/workflow.md`, `docs/design-claims.md`, and `docs/skill-reference.md`), and a comment in the edited file itself, each counting where it states why the shape is as it is. Only a shape none of them gives a reason for triggers the read. It skips the history read wherever the project's own documentation already holds the reason. That treats the record as a fallback for undocumented shapes only, which keeps the read's cost lowest without counting a bare description as a reason. The set of documents it covers is open-ended, so a runner cannot tell when it has looked far enough to skip the read, and two runners can disagree on the same file. That makes the trigger untestable in the sense the design draft asked for ("the trigger is testable without the record"). It also departs furthest from the goal's wording, and it still lets a document's account, which may be out of date, stand in for the task commits' bars.

The explanation condition is dropped: every file the task edits rather than creates triggers the `tasks <path> --with-body` read, whatever `requirements.md` or the context file says about it. No document counts as explaining, and the runner judges nothing before reading. The trigger becomes fully mechanical. A transcript shows whether it was met from the edits alone, so the field measurement needs no reader to judge which runs met it, and no past decision is missed because a document's account of the file was incomplete or stale. It contradicts the goal's recorded trigger and would need a goal revision. It also pays the full read on every edit of an existing file, prints of tens of kilobytes on the most-changed files that grow with every task, unless a bound is placed on large reads, an axis the sibling question on large reads owns.

The procedure takes no position on the context file. The trigger sentence keeps the goal's wording, a shape `requirements.md` does not explain, with no clause saying whether the context file or any other document counts, so each runner decides for itself whether something it read elsewhere explains the shape. It adds no prose and no rule to the procedure. Runners use their judgment of what they already hold, and the field measurement can show how they actually read the trigger before the wording is fixed. Runners will read the trigger differently. The measurement cannot tell a read skipped because the runner judged the context file sufficient from a read skipped for no reason, and whether that matters depends on how the measured run population is defined, an axis a sibling question owns. The question stays open in the runtime prose rather than being settled.

open-question.question: With the milestones tool unchanged, does the completion procedure bound its `tasks <path> --with-body` read on a file that many task commits changed, or is the read taken whole whatever it prints? Measured on 2026-11-10 it prints 200 lines (59,079 bytes) for `docs/skill-reference.md` and 104 lines (31,521 bytes) for `CLAUDE.md`, and it grows with every later task that changes the file.

Does the completion procedure's `tasks <path> --with-body` read carry the clause the review pass and the starting-state procedure put on their milestones-tool calls — the command written out in full, never through a variable, alias, or function of the runner's own — or does it show the full command with no such clause, as the other nine runtime files calling the milestones tool do?
open-question.alternative: `core/shared/complete-procedure.md` shows the full fixed command `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body` and puts the starting-state procedure's clause on it once, in the sentence that introduces the read: every milestones-tool call the read makes, the `tasks` call on each file it is taken for and the `show <milestone path>` follow-up alike, is written out in full on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function of the runner's own defined to stand for the command or any part of it. The `CLAUDE.md` shell-literal invariant gains the completion procedure among the sites carrying the clause, and the rebuilt host trees carry the sentence. The read qualifies under the invariant's own scoping rule, since a runner that takes it may call the tool several times in one task (one `tasks` per edited file, then `show`), and it runs in the population most given to rewriting commands, the completion agents of whom about three in four wrote an ad-hoc script in the 202 measured runs; a tool command held in a variable runs as one word naming no command under zsh, so the clause guards exactly the shortening this runner is likeliest to make, and it puts the procedure on the same footing as the other two discretionary multi-call readers of the milestones tool. It adds a sentence and an invariant entry for a failure no completion run has yet shown on this read, and it makes the clause no longer a marker of the two runners that call the tool on every pass; a measured run that wraps the command in a variable then reads as breaking a stated rule rather than as evidence of whether the clause was needed, which bears on what the field measurement's outcomes tell apart (owned by the sibling questions on measured outcomes).

`core/shared/complete-procedure.md` shows the full fixed command `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body`, and names `show <milestone path>` as its follow-up, with no sentence about writing the command out in full or never through a variable, alias, or function, as the nine other runtime files calling the milestones tool show theirs. The `CLAUDE.md` shell-literal invariant's list of clause sites stays unchanged. It keeps the procedure's addition to the read itself and leaves the shell-literal invariant untouched, the rule staying scoped to the sites where the failure was seen or where the tool is called on every pass; the discretionary read is called at most a few times per task on one quoted path, so no path list can be split, and the field measurement then observes unprompted whether completion runners shorten this command, which is the evidence a later clause would rest on. The read is a multi-call use of a tool command by the runners most prone to rewriting commands, the case the invariant's rationale names, so a runner that holds the command in a variable gets a call naming no command under zsh, and a discretionary read that fails that way may simply be dropped or replaced by a hand-composed `git log`, a deviation the measurement would then count against the read itself; how such a failure is handled is owned by the sibling question on a failed past-work read.

open-question.question: In the field measurement that decides whether the completion procedure's read of past work stays discretionary, which completion runs is the read counted against: every completion run, only runs that edited a file that already existed, or only runs a reader judges to have met the trigger (an edited file whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain), which no transcript shows mechanically?
open-question.alternative: The read is counted against every completion run in the measured run set, whatever the task touched. No trigger filter is applied: a run that only created files counts the same as one that edited files with a long history. Fully mechanical and impossible to argue with. Every `Task-completion:` commit and every completion transcript is in the population, so the denominator needs no diff parse and no judgment, and anyone re-running the scripts gets the same count. The trigger is a file the task edits rather than creates whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain, so every run that never met it counts as one where the read was not taken. That dilutes the rate with correct non-reads. Under a rule keyed on any miss or a share of runs, the read could be made required just because many tasks only create files, which the discretionary design meant to allow.

The read is counted only against runs that modified a file that already existed. This is read mechanically from each run's `Task-completion:` commit as a path with modify status (`git diff --diff-filter=M` on the commit, or the equivalent from the transcript's edit calls). The milestone's own `TASKS_TODO.md`, which every completion commit modifies, and the milestone's other files are left out. Whether `requirements.md` explains the file's shape is not judged. It follows the half of the trigger that can be checked by machine, edited rather than created, so runs that only created files no longer count as misses. It stays reproducible from the commits alone, with no reader in the loop and no transcript interpretation. It still counts runs whose edited file `requirements.md` does explain, where skipping the read is the correct behaviour, so it overstates misses. How much depends on how often tasks edit files the milestone's own decisions already describe. Whether a deleted, renamed, or moved file joins the population depends on how the trigger for removed files is settled, and that is a sibling question.

The read is counted only against runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded, as above) whose path `requirements.md` does not mention, as that file stood at the run's start. The mention test is a mechanical text search of the requirements file at the commit's parent. It stands in for "does not explain", and no reader judges the shape. It tracks both halves of the trigger while staying a script: a file the milestone's decisions name is presumed explained. So it removes the most obvious correct non-reads without any reader judgment, and the count can be re-run later. Being mentioned is not the same as being explained. A decision can name a file without accounting for its shape, and a shape can be explained without its path ever appearing (by module name, by a directory, or in the context file), so the proxy misclassifies in both directions in ways nobody has measured. Whether a context-file explanation should count is a sibling question's axis that the proxy ignores either way.

The read is counted only against runs that a reader judges to have met the trigger. Among the runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded), the reader reads `requirements.md` as it stood at the run's start and decides, per edited file, whether it explains that file's shape. Only runs with at least one unexplained edited file are counted. It measures exactly what the procedure asks of the runner, so a miss means a run that should have read past work and did not. That is the cleanest evidence for or against making the read required. No transcript shows the trigger mechanically, so the population rests on judgment for every edited-file run. That costs reading time on every such run, invites the measurer's bias about the outcome into the denominator, and may not be reproducible when the figures are checked again later. What counts as explained also depends on how the context-file trigger question is settled.

The population starts as the mechanical set of runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded). Every such run that took a history read counts as is. Only the runs that took no read are judged against `requirements.md` as it stood at the run's start, and a run whose edited files it explained is dropped from the population. Judgment is spent only where it changes the verdict, on the runs that would otherwise count as misses. That is a small share of the reader's effort compared with judging every run, and it still keeps correct non-reads from being counted as failures. The two sides are tested differently. A run that read past work without needing to is kept, while an equivalent run that skipped it is dropped, so the read rate is biased upward. The judged half carries the same reproducibility and bias risk as fully reader-judged counting.

The read is counted against more than one population at once: every completion run, and the mechanical subset that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded). Optionally a third, the reader-judged trigger subset, is added over the same runs. Each count is reported side by side in the measurement's result. It shows how much the trigger narrows the population and how the rate changes from one population to the next, so a later reader can tell a real miss rate from dilution. The mechanical populations stay reproducible even if the judged one is not. It does not settle which population the decision is made on. That rule has to name one, and naming it is part of the result-requiring-the-read question, a sibling. Without it, the side-by-side figures leave room to pick whichever population supports the preferred outcome. Each extra population also adds counting work.

open-question.question: In the field measurement that decides whether the completion procedure's read of past work stays discretionary, which outcomes are told apart for each counted run — for instance the named `tasks` command run as shown, a history read the agent composed itself (`git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` on the file), and no history read at all?

Over which runs is the field measurement of the completion procedure's read of past work taken: which projects and hosts, starting from which plugin release, and how many completion runs at the least before its result is read?

What measured result makes the completion procedure's read of past work a required step instead of a discretionary one: any counted run in which the read was not taken or was composed by hand, a stated share of the counted runs, or another rule?

Where are the scripts and the report of the field measurement of the completion procedure's read of past work kept, so that its figures can be checked again later: under the git-ignored `temp/`, where the reports and scripts of the two earlier field measurements stood and no longer do, in a tracked location, or does the plan in `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` leave it unstated?
